China has agreed to increase weekly flight limits with Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, while a separate deal between the two Central Asian neighbours will allow more services on regional routes.

The agreements were reached during the third meeting of the Central Asia–China (C5+1) Working Group on Civil Aviation Cooperation, held in Tashkent.

Uzbekistan and China agreed to raise the limit on weekly flights between the two countries from 100 to 114.

Kazakhstan reached a separate agreement with China to increase its permitted weekly frequencies from 150 to 180, while adding Chengdu and Kashgar to the list of destinations airlines are authorised to serve.

Building the 'Air Silk Road'

The latest agreements build on the "Air Silk Road" initiative, which aims to open new routes and make it easier for airlines to operate across borders.

In January 2024, Uzbekistan's Ministry of Transport and the Civil Aviation Administration of China signed an agreement to jointly develop the initiative.

Uzbekistan now wants travellers flying from China and neighbouring Central Asian countries to Europe to be able to change planes at its airports, according to Jamoliddin Nazarov, Head of the Air Transport Department at the country's Ministry of Transport.

Kyrgyzstan signed its own memorandum with China under the initiative in 2024.

"In 2025, working together with our Chinese colleagues, we opened a new air corridor," said Qanat Tologonov, Deputy Director of Kyrgyzstan's State Civil Aviation Agency.

In April 2026, China's Chengdu Airlines launched a weekly direct service between Kashgar in western China and Osh, Kyrgyzstan's second-largest city, using a Chinese-made C909 aircraft.

In Kazakhstan, airlines want to serve more Chinese cities beyond major hubs such as Beijing and Shanghai, according to Saltanat Tompiyeva, Chair of the country's Civil Aviation Committee.

Expanding air travel within Central Asia

The Tashkent meeting also produced agreements covering flights between Central Asian countries themselves.

Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan agreed to raise the permitted number of weekly flights between Tashkent and both Almaty and Astana from 42 to 60 on each route. The limit on other routes between the two countries will increase from 14 to 20 flights a week.

Kazakhstan's Civil Aviation Committee says the changes will help meet growing demand for travel between the two countries.

Vietjet Qazaqstan launched direct flights from Astana to Bishkek and Samarkand in November 2025, increasing frequencies on both routes in early 2026.

Adilbek Umraliyev, the airline's CEO, told Euronews that further opportunities exist in smaller regional destinations, highlighting Bukhara and Samarkand for their "quite significant tourism potential".

For airlines considering additional cross-border routes, operating costs remain a concern.

Umraliyev said rising fuel prices and airport charges are making regional flights more expensive to operate.

He called for closer cooperation between aviation authorities and airlines to address these costs and make cross-border travel more affordable.

Passenger demand is another consideration, particularly for smaller cities seeking regular international flights.

"There needs to be sufficient passenger traffic, business activity and economic demand in each country," Tologonov said.

People with type 2 diabetes who stopped GLP-1 treatment had twice the risk of heart attack, stroke or death than those who continued, according to a new study.

Breakthrough medicines used for cutting weight and addressing diabetes mimic the natural GLP-1 hormone to regulate blood sugar and curb appetite. In recent years, they have become a cornerstone of treatment for type 2 diabetes and obesity, also showing benefits for heart and kidney health.

Despite their proven effects, a substantial proportion of patients stop taking these drugs, often within the first year. Common reasons include gastrointestinal side effects, perceived lack of efficacy, high costs, and concern about rare side effects.

Coming off treatment is frequently followed by weight regain and a worsening of several cardiometabolic risk factors, such as blood sugar and blood pressure.

Now, a new study, published in The Lancet Regional Health Europe, found that stopping such medicines was linked to a doubled combined risk of non-fatal heart attack, non-fatal stroke, or death from any cause compared to those who continued. This equates to roughly four events per 100 people per year among those who stopped, compared with two per 100 among those who continued.

Among those who stopped treatment, the risks were higher for people with obesity than for those without. People with obesity (a body mass index above 30) had a 127% higher cardiovascular risk after coming off GLP-1s, compared with a 61% increase among those without obesity.

However, because it was an observational study, it cannot determine whether discontinuing GLP-1s directly causes the increased risk or whether people who stopped were already in poorer health.

After people stopped treatment, their weight, blood sugar and blood pressure changed only slightly, and there were no significant differences between those who suffered a heart attack, stroke or death and those who didn’t. This suggests these factors may not fully explain the higher risk, the authors noted.

The researchers analysed electronic medical records from more than 300 diabetes clinics in the Italian Association of Clinical Diabetologists database. The records covered over 80,000 people with type 2 diabetes and no established cardiovascular disease who had started a GLP-1 between 2004 and 2024.

The majority of participants received earlier-generation GLP-1s. Semaglutide — one of the most common new-generation treatments — accounted for only a minor fraction of use, and tirzepatide was not included because it entered the Italian market after the study period.

People who continued treatment took a GLP-1 for nearly three years on average, compared with just over one year for those who stopped.

The authors say the findings suggest that, in people with type 2 diabetes and no established cardiovascular disease, long-term GLP-1 use may be important for maintaining overall health benefits. They noted that further research is needed to determine whether stopping directly contributes to increased cardiovascular risk or is instead a marker of worsening health or underlying cardiovascular risk.

At the Leaders’ Summit, heads of state pose for a ‘family photo’ and make speeches setting out their countries’ climate priorities, announcing commitments and, often, putting pressure on other countries to act.

New research by the European Travel Commission finds that more Europeans have autumn and winter travel plans, with remote destinations and increased getaways shaping intentions.

New data has found that 76% of Europeans plan to take an overnight trip between October 2026 and March 2027 – a 3% increase compared to last year.

According to the latest Monitoring Sentiment for Intra-European Travel Autumn and Winter 2026/2027 report, issued by the European Travel Commission (ETC), city breaks, culture trips and festive getaways are driving the demand.

Based on an online survey of 6,000 respondents from Germany, United Kingdom, France, Netherlands, Italy, Belgium, Switzerland, Spain, Poland and Austria, who had taken at least two overnight trips during the last three years, travel intentions are expected to peak around Christmas time, with 23% of respondents planning a trip during the festive period.

Visiting friends and family is a strong motivation for December travel according to 34% of respondents – compared with 10% across other months. After a dip in January, travel is expected to pick up again across February and March (29%).

“It is particularly encouraging to see an increase in intention during February and March, typically quieter periods of the year, as well as a growing interest in off-the-beaten-track destinations,” Eduardo Santander, Chief Executive Officer of the ETC, said.

“These two trends combined could be leveraged to reduce tourism congestion and create new opportunities for local businesses in established and developing destinations alike.”

The report also found that single-destination stays remain the trip format of choice, favoured by 60% of travellers. This preference is especially notable for those seeking sun and beach (69%), skiing (67%) and city breaks (66%).

Despite strong travel intentions, financial pressures (37%) and geopolitical instability (23%) are the leading concerns for would-be travellers. Extreme weather (10%) and overcrowding (9%) also feature among their worries.

Further, when it comes to deciding where to travel to, safety is the most important consideration (20%), with the Polish (45%), British and Spanish (both at 43%) respondents being the top markets that only avoid direct safety risks.

Other considerations include pleasant weather (15%), as well as attractive prices and destinations that are low-cost (14% and 11%).

Where is everyone planning to travel?

France, Spain, Italy, Germany and the UK are the top countries among respondents, with the ETC finding that 64% are keen on intra-European travel.

Southern Europe and the Mediterranean remain popular choices, with 53% intending to visit the region this autumn and winter.

Meanwhile, western Europe is gaining ground, attracting positive sentiment from 23% of respondents, marking a 5% increase compared to last year. The region is especially popular for sun and beach (25%), culture and heritage (18%) and city breaks (16%).

At the same time, there is a growing interest in Europe’s “less popular” destinations, with 54% attracted to remote or "off-the-beaten-track" spots. The Netherlands, Switzerland, Poland, Belgium and Austria are the top five in this regard.

Among the 4,555 respondents who said they were likely to travel in the next six months, Poland, Spain, the Netherlands and Germany emerged as the most popular destinations.

More Europeans are also securing their travel arrangements in advance, with 38% of travellers having either partially booked or arranged their next trip's accommodation or transport, or booked all components of their next trip. This is up by 5% compared to last year's survey.

Leisure, city breaks and cultural heritage

While single-city itineraries proved to be the most popular travel format, the ETC found that 36% of respondents said they plan to visit multiple cities within one country for their next trip, and a further 4% intend to visit multiple countries this season.

Leisure is the leading motivation driving travel intentions at 71%, with Italy, Belgium and the Netherlands ranking as the top destinations for such getaways. This season of leisure getaways will also be marked by city breaks (19%), culture and heritage (18%), as well as travellers seeking sun and beach (18%).

When it comes to experiences, travellers are most looking forward to enjoying natural landscapes (19%), gastronomy (16%) and diving into local culture (15%) during their next trip in Europe.

City breaks are especially popular for travellers across October and November (23%), while culture and heritage getaways are favoured during February to March. In both instances, travellers typically budget between €501 to €1,000 (30% and 28%) across a four to six nights' stay (39% and 46%).

The focus on security architecture has struck a nerve among Europeans, who suspect Russia is using it as a ploy to divert intention from Ukraine and gain a bigger say on the continent's decision-making.

These days, two words are enough to unsettle Europeans: security architecture.

The issue has moved to the heart of negotiations aimed at ending Russia's war on Ukraine after US President Donald Trump teased a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe".

The comment was followed by an extensive social media post from his special envoy, Jared Kushner, in which he laid down several principles to create a "more stable and predictable security environment" on the continent.

Kushner's message notably sidestepped the fact that Moscow has launched a full-scale invasion against a sovereign, internationally recognised nation and instead blamed "decades of mistrust" and "competing security concerns" between Europe and Russia.

"For more than 30 years, Europe and Russia have struggled to establish a sustainable security framework," he wrote.

The wording rattled Europeans, who quickly pointed out that it was not they but Russia who "struggled" to uphold the architecture built in the previous century.

"We have European security architecture in place," High Representative Kaja Kallas said on Monday during a G7 meeting in Paris.

"The only one who is breaching that security architecture is Russia. That is why we have to make sure that in those talks there are clear concessions from the Russian side, because otherwise we will just see more of these attacks."

Russia's war on Ukraine is considered to have breached, among others, the 1975 Helsinki Accords and the 1990 Paris Charter, which provide the basis for the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE); the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which prohibits Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defence; and the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, which safeguards the territorial integrity "of all states".

Russia has also been accused of committing war crimes, including the crime of aggression, in blatant disregard of international law.

"Europe does not need a new security architecture, as Russia wants us to believe, but rather the simple restoration of the existing security architecture," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, echoing Kallas's point.

Speaking in Romania, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen cautioned that "any meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture can only be undertaken once a ceasefire in Ukraine has been achieved".

This, she noted, must happen only with Europe at the table.

"An arrangement about the future of Ukraine and of Europe above our heads would not just be unwise. It is actually impossible," Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said.

'Doing Putin's bidding'

The collective pushback comes as Europeans try to restore diplomacy after the alarming events of October, which saw Trump strike a diesel supply deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, ease longstanding sanctions on Moscow and bitterly attack Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The rapid sequence shocked Europe and revived fears that Trump and Putin would thrash out a secret deal to secure Ukraine's capitulation. Trump's promise of a "big, beautiful agreement" encompassing all of Europe fit in with the suspicions.

Putin has never hidden his intense distaste for NATO, the alliance forged after World War II to build deterrence through collective defence.

In the weeks leading up to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia issued an ultimatum to NATO to stop its eastward expansion and withdraw troops from members that joined after 1997. The demands were outright rejected. A few months after the war erupted, Finland and Sweden, two historically neutral countries, applied to join NATO.

Despite the setback, Putin has never given up on his plan to "destroy" NATO and deal with European countries separately, says Judy Dempsey, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, who believes the talk plays directly into Russia's hands.

"This is an attempt by the Kremlin and President Trump to actually bypass NATO and redraw the security architecture of Europe. This is also an attempt to break the link for the transatlantic alliance, the bedrock of which is NATO," Dempsey said.

"Trump is doing Putin's bidding," she added. "Europeans have to say no to this. We have one architecture: it's called NATO. There's no reason at all to change it. The only reason it's under threat is that Russia is attacking Ukraine at full blast."

European officials involved in the peace process have noticed Russia's keen interest in the security architecture, which they see as a ploy to divert attention from the core issues on the table: the cessation of hostilities and security guarantees for Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly refused to establish a ceasefire, even temporary and targeted, and opposed the deployment of Western troops inside Ukraine after the war. Meanwhile, it has ramped up airstrikes to freeze Ukrainians ahead of winter.

By contrast, Moscow has openly spoken about the broader picture, almost as if Ukraine were a footnote in the story. Putin regularly refers to "the root causes of the conflict", a codename for NATO's eastward expansion, and his foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, highlights the need to build a "new security architecture" on the Eurasian continent.

For Europeans, this discourse reflects great-power aspirations to expand Russia's sphere of influence and gain decision-making powers, in particular a veto on NATO's future membership, to which it is simply not entitled.

"Russia is interested in discussing Europe's security architecture because it wants greater leverage over European decisions on Ukraine," Natia Seskuria, a senior research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), said.

"By broadening the negotiations, Moscow seeks to make Ukraine's future a secondary question within a larger bargain over Russia's relationship with Europe."

Adding the security architecture to the already long list of topics in the peace talks risks dragging down the process, complicating a final settlement and driving a wedge between NATO allies, all of which would benefit Russian interests.

"Russia could also use the discussion to deepen divisions between the US and its European allies over deterrence, Europe's future security arrangements and the scope of guarantees for Ukraine," Seskuria said.

"By exploiting differences over what concessions are acceptable, Moscow could weaken the cohesion needed both to negotiate an effective agreement and to sustain it."

Just as the alarm reached its peak ahead of a new round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi, the US and Europe released a statement saying that "a strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defence".

Anthropic plans to raise up to $64 billion (€57.1bn) in its upcoming initial public offering, the artificial intelligence giant said in a filing on Tuesday, in a listing that could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion (€1.25trn).

The stock market debut will be the first by one of the leading AI model developers and is being seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last.

The maker of the Claude AI models said in a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission that it aims to sell 825 million shares at between $70 and $78 each (€62.44–€69.58). The shares will trade under the ticker "ANT."

Seven tech companies including Google, Nvidia, AMD and Microsoft have also agreed to buy $26 billion (€23.2bn) of non-voting shares at the IPO price in a separate private placement, the filing showed.

The companies are investors in Anthropic or major suppliers of its computing power.

Anthropic had been expected to raise up to $100 billion (€89.2bn), which would have made it the largest IPO on record.

Even at the top of its price range, the offering would fall short of the record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $86 billion (€76.7bn) in its June IPO at a valuation of $1.77 trillion (€1.58trn).

Anthropic has been aiming to go public the week of November 16, and reports said its shares would begin trading on November 19.

Anthropic's listing is "just another chapter" in investors' worries over the cost of the AI buildout and how it gets financed, Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth Management, told AFP.

"But at the end of the day, I think there are three massive companies that investors have wanted to be part of for the last three years and that’s SpaceX for sure, Anthropic is next, and perhaps next year OpenAI," he said.

The listing comes as Wall Street digests the results of the US midterm elections, in which Democrats, who are more wary of AI, won control of both chambers of Congress and have vowed to put the brakes on President Donald Trump's agenda.

The slide has brought volatility to shares of companies linked to the AI boom, with AI chip-maker Nvidia particularly in focus after chief executive Jensen Huang was caught up in a spy scandal.

'Catastrophic risks'

The company’s revenue reached $17 billion (€15.2bn) in the third quarter, up from $1.4 billion (€1.25bn) a year earlier, according to the filing.

Its annualized run-rate revenue was about $81 billion (€72.3bn) as of October 31, up $10 billion (€8.9 billion) from the end of September, the company said. This figure describes how much the company expects in a year based on current revenue.

Estimates in recent months had put Anthropic’s valuation as high as $2 trillion (€1.78trn), but they have slipped along with a slide in AI stocks on Wall Street.

Anthropic's IPO filing devotes extensive space to the technology’s risks, including concerns that advanced AI systems "could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."

The company also warns that its public positions on AI regulation and safety could expose it to “political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action.”

This referred to feuds with the Trump White House. The Pentagon has labeled Anthropic a national security risk after the company refused to lift restrictions on military use of its technology.

Its stratospheric costs have also been underlined, with Anthropic committing hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity. It warned that it must make many of those payments even if demand falls short.

Under the governance structure laid out in the filings, the seven co-founders, led by chief executive Dario Amodei and his sister, president Daniela Amodei, will keep just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, so outside investors cannot outvote them.

US Democrats suffered a blow on Tuesday as Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's impeachment over the war waged on Iran.

The House failed to secure the votes needed to send the impeachment resolution to the Judiciary Committee, with a vote of 211 to 204, handing President Donald Trump a victory just days after his party's disastrous midterm election defeat. Democrats and some Republicans had been hoping to hold a vote on Wednesday, which would have seen Hegseth face formal charges.

The resolution was formally proposed by Trump critic, Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie, who was the only member of his party to oppose the procedural manoeuvre, according to US media.

Republicans currently hold a majority in the House, but this will end in January, when Democrats are expected to take control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump's party's midterm defeat comes amid widespread discontent among the US public over the country's war on Iran, as well as soaring gas prices and the rising cost of living.

Trump took to his social media platform, TRUTH Social, to express his strong support for Hegseth, describing him as a "Great American Patriot" who had been exonerated.

Meanwhile, earlier on Tuesday, Hegseth called the attempt to impeach him a "farce" while defending the military operations he has carried out under Trump, as well as the war on Iran.

During a Pentagon press conference, he said, "It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," branding the accusations as "slander" and "sabotage".

Following Hegseth's television appearance, Trump once again showed his support through a TRUTH Social post, writing, "Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS."

Vice President JD Vance also commented, saying that Hegseth had "obviously not" committed impeachable offences.

Massie's eight articles of impeachment

The eight articles of impeachment brought against Hegseth by Massie include several allegations concerning the handling of the Iran war, including waging war without congressional authorisation and abuse of power as Pentagon chief.

They also include allegations surrounding strikes carried out against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, which Massie described as "extrajudicial killings", as well as the 2025 conflict with Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.

Massie also accused Hegseth of suppressing free speech after he attempted to punish Democratic Senator Mark Kelly over a video in which Kelly urged military and intelligence personnel to stand up against illegal orders.

Democrats will be able to revive impeachment efforts once they take control of Congress in January. At the same time, Massie will be leaving Congress after losing his Republican primary to a Trump-backed challenger.
